title: Smile
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss smiling: the facial muscles involved (zygomaticus major, orbicularis oculi), the Duchenne smile (AU6 plus AU12) and Guillaume Duchenne's electrical facial stimulation experiments, whether fake smiles can be detected by the eyes, primate and chimpanzee bared-teeth displays, infant smiling and social smiling, blind infants and congenitally blind athletes, cross-cultural interpretation of facial expressions (Paul Ekman's universal expressions), smiling in portraits and yearbooks and photography history, Ekman's categories of smiles (miserable, embarrassment, reward, dominant, affiliative, coordination, uncanny), whether smiling makes you happy (pen-in-mouth studies, Korb electrical study, DBT half smile), and a listener mail correction about the Red Baron's death. The episode includes live-show plugs and a sponsor-style promo at the start.

entities.name: I Don't Feel at Home in This World Anymore

segments.title: Intro and live show plug
segments.summary: Hosts plug their Virgin Voyages cruise live show to Bermuda and introduce the topic of smiling.

segments.title: Smiling muscles and the frown myth
segments.summary: Smiling is muscle movement; facial muscles are fast twitch fibers; the claim that frowning takes more muscles than smiling is not verified; dentist websites repeat it.

segments.title: Facial action coding system and Duchenne smile
segments.summary: Facial action coding system names muscle movements; AU12 (zygomaticus major) is in all smiles; AU6 (orbicularis oculi) involves the eyes; together they form the Duchenne smile.

segments.title: Guillaume Duchenne and fake smiles
segments.summary: Duchenne used electrical stimulation on faces and photographed results; he claimed eyes reveal genuine smiles, but that is probably not true, and people can voluntarily produce eye smiles, though debated.

segments.title: Primate smiling and submission
segments.summary: Primates are more facially expressive than humans; bared-teeth displays in chimpanzees signal submission, which carries over into human smiling for appeasement.

segments.title: Bowling smile study and infant smiling
segments.summary: A 1979 bowling study found people smiled more while talking than after strikes. Newborns smile randomly, social smiling starts around six to twelve weeks, and infants time smiles to get caretaker attention.

segments.title: Prenatal carrot and kale study
segments.summary: A 2022 Journal of Psychological Science study gave pregnant women carrot or kale pills; babies smiled after carrot and grimaced after kale.

segments.title: Congenitally blind infants and athletes
segments.summary: Blind infants smile in response to voices like sighted babies; blind Paralympic athletes from 23 cultures show similar spontaneous expressions; children masked disappointment with smiles similarly regardless of sight. A tangent about an actress follows.

segments.title: Ekman's universal expressions
segments.summary: Paul Ekman's 1960s studies proposed universal facial expressions (anger, disgust, enjoyment, fear, sadness, surprise, later contempt); critics note multiple-choice method flaws, but subsequent research largely finds agreement on meanings.

segments.title: Cultural differences in smiling
segments.summary: Smiling is more common in immigrant countries like the US and Brazil; East Asian emoticons use eyes; a 2015 study across 44 cultures found smiles associated with intelligence in some countries and lower intelligence in others.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: History of smiling in portraits and photography
segments.summary: Portrait painting's serious faces, etiquette manuals discouraging showing teeth, the Laughing Cavalier, smiles as signs of immaturity or insanity in European art, and the rise of smiling in US photographs after the 1930s via camera advertising.

segments.title: Yearbook photos and smiling
segments.summary: Yearbook smiles took time to catch on; by the 1930s smiling became common, and by the 1950s yearbook photos were smiling.

segments.title: Ekman's types of smiles
segments.summary: Ekman identified smile types. Real enjoyment smiles involve eye cover fold; hosts discuss reward, affiliative, dominant, miserable, and embarrassment smiles.

segments.title: Coordination smile and movie tangents
segments.summary: Coordination smile exemplified by William H. Macy in Fargo; tangents on movie length and other films.

segments.title: Uncanny smile
segments.summary: Uncanny smile in horror films such as Jack Nicholson in The Shining, Insidious; the eyes and mouth mismatch is unsettling, though little science exists.

segments.title: Does smiling make you happy?
segments.summary: Darwin linked facial expression to feelings; the 1988 pen-in-mouth study with cartoons; a 2024 Korb study using electrical stimulation; critics note reliance on self-report; DBT half smile technique.

segments.title: Service workers and surface acting
segments.summary: Service employees who must fake smiles may drink more heavily, a claim social psychologists treat cautiously.

segments.title: Listener mail and Red Baron correction
segments.summary: A listener notes a live show in Ottawa and Canadian tour dates; a correction says the Red Baron was likely killed by Australian ground fire rather than Eddie Rickenbacker, and Rickenbacker did not see combat until the month he died.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and iHeartRadio production note.
